title: Housing vouchers and neighborhood choice
summary: We studied a change in how housing voucher rent limits are set, and whether it affected where voucher households lived.
question: In 2018, the Small Area Fair Market Rent policy changed how rent limits were set for housing vouchers. Did that change where Housing Choice Voucher households were concentrated?
approach: Built a census-tract panel covering 2014 to 2022 using HUD housing data, then compared Dallas County with Harris County.
Used difference-in-differences with tract and year fixed effects. We also checked trends with an event study and mapped the data with GeoPandas.
Looked at voucher concentration alongside neighborhood racial composition and poverty.
takeaway: We found an association between the policy change and lower voucher concentration in the treatment area. The trends before the policy were different across the two counties, though, which makes it difficult to say how much of the change was caused by the policy itself.
limitation: HUD suppresses small household counts, and these data don’t tell us where individual households moved. Along with the differences in pre-policy trends, those gaps limit what we can conclude.
credits: Team: Lingyue Hao, He Jiang, Ammy Lin, Myla Simmons, and Anvita Suresh.

title: Training sparse neural networks
summary: How many neural network connections do we actually need? We compared three sparse training methods on CIFAR-10.
question: We wanted to see how much we could reduce a neural network’s connections while keeping its predictive accuracy. We also compared methods that keep the same connections with methods that change them during training.
approach: Compared fixed sparse masks, Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET), and gradient-guided RigL on a CIFAR-style ResNet-20.
Trained at 90%, 95%, and 98% sparsity, using both SGD with momentum and Adam.
Compared accuracy curves and weight visualizations, and looked at how connections changed during training.
takeaway: Static sparsity was a competitive baseline in our experiments, and RigL generally did better than SET. The optimizer made a difference, too. At the highest sparsity level, the model had clearer limits on what it could learn.
limitation: We used one model family and CIFAR-10, with no data augmentation and only 15 training epochs. These results describe those runs; they don’t establish which method would work best in other settings.
credits: Team: Ammy Lin, Tonantzin Real Rojas, and Anvita Suresh. Completed for Introduction to Deep Learning at Duke University.

title: Sparkify: music recommendations
summary: A music recommendation pipeline built with Airflow, PostgreSQL, and Streamlit. We used simulated listening data to test how the pieces worked together.
role: I worked on exploratory analysis, Airflow DAGs, the Streamlit dashboard, the recommendation model, and team coordination. These responsibilities were shared with teammates; the repository has the full breakdown.
question: How do we turn track metadata and listening history into recommendations that can be updated on a schedule and viewed in a dashboard?
approach: Combined public track metadata with generated users and synthetic listening events.
Used Airflow to schedule data ingestion, embedding generation, and recommendation updates, with PostgreSQL for storage.
Built a Streamlit dashboard to view the recommendations and added Python tests and workflow checks.
takeaway: The model was one part of the project. We also connected data preparation, scheduled inference, storage, and validation so the recommendations could make it into a dashboard people could use.
limitation: The listening histories are simulated, so we haven’t shown how well these recommendations would work for real listeners. We also haven’t tested the synchronous inference approach with a large user population.
credits: Team: Jordan, Aesha, Ammy, and Tonantzin. We shared work on the model, orchestration, dashboard, and testing; the repository lists our responsibilities.

title: Modeling flood risk
summary: For this class project, we used synthetic data to compare flood-risk models and try out payout rules for parametric insurance.
role: I was the Project Manager and Risk Strategist. The repository lists each team member’s role.
question: For insurance that pays out when specified conditions are met, how do we choose rules that are understandable and reliable? We used a flood-risk example to look at that question alongside model accuracy.
approach: Compared linear regression, XGBoost, and sparse optimal decision trees using 20 features describing the environment, infrastructure, land use, and governance.
Used SHAP to examine feature importance, then tested sensitivity to reporting bias and changes in feature distributions.
Simulated tiered payout rules and compared thresholds for different stakeholder priorities.
takeaway: We compared models alongside the payout rules they might support. The simulations also let us try different thresholds depending on which stakeholder priorities we wanted to emphasize.
limitation: All of the data are synthetic. The feature rankings and payout rules are experimental, and would need to be checked against credible real-world data before being used for insurance or disaster response.
credits: Team: Lingyue Hao, He Jiang, Ammy Lin, Myla Simmons, and Anvita Suresh. Completed for IDS 705: Machine Learning at Duke University.

title: Simulating credit portfolio losses
summary: Using Monte Carlo simulation to see how default probabilities and correlations between borrowers affect a credit portfolio’s losses.
question: What happens to portfolio losses when borrowers are more likely to default at the same time? We looked at how default probabilities and correlations changed the loss distribution.
approach: Started with the public Default of Credit Card Clients dataset as the basis for the portfolio.
Used a Vasicek one-factor model, with a shared systematic factor and borrower-specific factors, to model defaults.
Simulated losses under different default-probability and correlation assumptions, then compared Value-at-Risk and Conditional Value-at-Risk.
takeaway: Expected loss doesn’t tell the whole story. In our simulations, changing the dependence between defaults could substantially change the tail of the loss distribution, where the largest losses occur.
limitation: The results depend on the one-factor model, the scenarios we chose, and a historical dataset. This was a classroom simulation, so it shouldn’t be read as a forecast of current credit losses.
credits: Team: Jordan Andrew, Ammy Lin, Farnoosh Memari, and Tonantzin Real Rojas. Completed for MATH 789 at Duke University.

title: The DNA dilemma
summary: What would you do if a company sold your genetic data? We designed a classroom discussion around four people with different stakes in that decision.
role: Tonantzin Real Rojas and I designed the scenarios and led the class discussion together. The web implementation was built with Gemini assistance, as credited in the repository.
question: A consumer, company executive, buyer, and data scientist might see the same genetic-data sale very differently. We wanted classmates to work through those perspectives and think about the responsibilities involved.
approach: Designed four stakeholder paths around a hypothetical genetic-data sale and what might follow from it.
Created branching choices about consent, privacy, research value, and responsibilities within an organization.
Added reflection prompts and a recap of each participant’s decisions for the class discussion.
takeaway: The point was to give classmates a set of decisions to work through, then a chance to discuss why they chose what they did. Taking on another role was part of that exercise.
limitation: The scenarios are hypothetical and inspired by real events. They’re teaching material for an ethics discussion, rather than a factual account or legal analysis of the 23andMe case.
credits: Discussion and scenario design: Ammy Lin and Tonantzin Real Rojas. Developed for IDS 704: Data Science Ethics and Policy at Duke University, with AI-assisted web implementation.
